findings.description: The inline user policy grants wildcard actions (ec2:*, s3:*, lambda:*, cloudwatch:*) on Resource "*", violating least privilege. Compromise of this user's static key would permit full control of compute, storage and serverless resources, including privilege escalation via ec2:RunInstances/iam:PassRole-adjacent paths, lambda function modification, and bulk data exfiltration from any S3 bucket in the account.

A permanent IAM access key/secret pair is provisioned for a user holding an account-wide wildcard policy. Long-lived static credentials attached to a highly privileged identity are a prime target for theft and lateral movement; a role with short-lived credentials should be used instead.

No pgp_key is supplied, so the secret access key is persisted in cleartext in the Terraform state file (encrypted_secret is only populated when a PGP key is given). Anyone with read access to state — including remote backends and CI artifacts — obtains fully privileged AWS credentials.

findings.issue_category: privileged IAM user instead of role
findings.description: A standalone IAM user is created with a directly attached wildcard inline policy and static programmatic credentials rather than a federated role with temporary credentials, and no MFA or rotation is enforced. This establishes a durable, unmanaged high-privilege identity outside role-based access control.

The access key secret attribute is exported as a root module output. Because no pgp_key is set the attribute is not encrypted, and outputs are readable via `terraform output`, propagated into parent modules, and frequently captured in CI/CD logs, widening exposure of the privileged credential.
